definition: An aluminum disc coated with nitrocellulose; the master groove is cut into the coating.
Spraying a thin conductive silver layer onto the lacquer, the same way a mirror is made, so it can be electroplated.
Growing nickel onto the silvered lacquer in a chemical bath with electric current to make metal copies of the groove.
The first nickel negative pulled off the lacquer, called the master in the UK. Its grooves are ridges. One US plant uses the word for an archive copy instead.
A metal positive plated from the father, with grooves like a record, used to grow stampers.
A thin nickel negative, about 145 grams, mounted in the press, one per side. Worn stampers are replaced from the mother.
How many generations of metal parts are made between lacquer and press. More steps means more stampers can come from one lacquer.
Cutting straight into copper instead of lacquer, which skips the lacquer and its plating.
The first few records off new stampers, usually four or five, sent to the artist and label for approval before the run.
The PVC mix records are pressed from, sold as pellets. Black comes from carbon black.
The warm lump of compound placed between the stampers, about three times as thick as the finished record.
The machine that heats compound and pushes it out, like toothpaste, to form the puck.
The excess vinyl squeezed out at the edge during pressing, trimmed off and recycled.
Drying center labels in an oven, often overnight, so moisture does not bubble them in the press.
A press whose molds are heated by electrically heated water instead of steam from a gas boiler.
The Vinyl Record Manufacturers Association of North America, founded after the 2020 Apollo Masters fire.
A heavier 12 inch LP. Standard weight is about 130-155 grams; 180 gram records use the same stampers and groove depth.
A color effect made by mixing pellets of different colors in one biscuit.
A printed image sealed under a thin clear playing surface on a PVC core, per a retailer's description.
Shooting molten plastic into a closed mold, as Sonopress does with PET for its EcoRecord, instead of compressing a PVC puck.
How fast the groove passes the stylus: about 21 inches per second at the outer edge of a 12 inch at 33 1/3, about 28.3 at 45.
